turns.message: What should I do if my tire is flat?
turns.answer:
If your tire is flat, slow down gradually and pull over somewhere safe, away from traffic. Turn on your hazard lights and don't keep driving on the flat tire.

Use the spare tire or repair kit as the owner's manual describes; a temporary spare has speed and distance limits. Do not drive on a tire with a sidewall cut or bulge.

A tire shop can tell whether a tread puncture can be repaired; sidewall damage usually means replacing the tire.

turns.message: How often should I check my tire pressure?
turns.answer:
Check the pressures at least once a month with the tires cold (before driving, or after a few minutes parked), using the figures on the sticker in the driver's door jamb or in the owner's manual for your exact car. Front and rear can differ, and many cars list a higher figure for a full load. Don't use the maximum printed on the tire: that's the tire's limit, not the car's setting.

Pressure loss, wear, alignment or suspension condition, loading, and usage can affect tire condition.

Inflate to the vehicle's placard pressure, not the maximum printed on the tire.

A bulge, exposed cords, rapid pressure loss, or tire damage can cause loss of control.

turns.message: What tire pressure should my Toyota Vios have?
turns.answer:
Check the pressures at least once a month with the tires cold (before driving, or after a few minutes parked), using the figures on the sticker in the driver's door jamb or in the owner's manual for your exact car. Front and rear can differ, and many cars list a higher figure for a full load. Don't use the maximum printed on the tire: that's the tire's limit, not the car's setting.

Inflate to the vehicle's placard pressure, not the maximum printed on the tire. Rotate the tires at the interval in the owner's manual.

A bulge, exposed cords, rapid pressure loss, or tire damage can cause loss of control.

turns.message: My tire blew out on the highway
turns.answer:
If a tire blows out, hold the steering wheel firmly and keep the car straight. Don't brake hard: ease off the accelerator, let the car slow down gradually, then steer to a safe place and stop.

Old or worn tires.

turns.message: There's a bulge on the sidewall of my tire
turns.answer:
A bulge, bubble or deep cut in the sidewall means the tire's internal structure is damaged and it can burst. Don't drive on it: stop safely and fit the spare or call roadside assistance.

Sidewall damage can't be repaired safely; the tire needs replacing.

turns.message: Why are my tires wearing on the inside edge?
turns.answer:
Uneven wear has typical patterns: both edges worn usually means under-inflation, the centre worn means over-inflation, one edge worn usually means misalignment, and patchy or cupped wear points to suspension or balance problems.

Wear concentrated on edges, the centre, one side or in patches.

Incorrect tire pressure. Skipped tire rotations.

Replace any tire worn down to its wear indicators or with exposed cords.

turns.message: What is tire rotation?
turns.answer:
Rotate the tires about every 8,000 to 10,000 km, conveniently at every second oil change, so they wear evenly and last longer. Follow the pattern in the owner's manual: some tires and cars need a specific one.

Combine rotation with a pressure and tread check.

turns.message: What is wheel balancing?
turns.answer:
Wheel balancing evens out the weight around each wheel and tire so they spin smoothly. Unbalanced wheels usually cause vibration through the steering wheel at certain speeds.

Have the wheels balanced when fitting new tires, after a puncture repair, or if vibration appears.

turns.message: Why is my car overheating?
turns.answer:
Overheating means the cooling system isn't removing heat fast enough, or coolant isn't circulating properly. An overheating indication means heat is not being removed or circulated as intended, or the temperature reading is not trustworthy.

A coolant-pump circulation or drive problem can reduce coolant flow and cause overheating at different speeds; leaks or noise may be present but are not required.

If the gauge is in the red or you see steam, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Never open the radiator cap while the engine is hot; hot coolant can cause severe burns.

turns.message: What if the coolant is full?
turns.answer: With the coolant full, the likely causes are a thermostat stuck closed, a radiator fan that isn't switching on, a weak water pump or a blocked radiator. Check whether the upper radiator hose gets hot: if it stays cool while the engine overheats, the thermostat is the prime suspect.

turns.message: My temperature gauge is going up
turns.answer:
An overheating indication means heat is not being removed or circulated as intended, or the temperature reading is not trustworthy. Treat a high-temperature warning as real until the vehicle-specific checks establish otherwise.

Less common but serious causes include internal leakage, combustion gases entering the cooling circuit, a restricted exhaust or other engine fault increasing heat load, or an inaccurate temperature sensor/gauge. These require evidence-based testing.

If the gauge is in the red or you see steam, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Never open the radiator cap while the engine is hot; hot coolant can cause severe burns.

turns.message: Is it safe to keep driving?
turns.answer:
No. Driving an overheating engine can quickly warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket. Stop, let it cool completely, and have it checked before driving on.

Do not continue driving an overheating vehicle; severe damage can occur.

turns.message: My engine is misfiring
turns.answer:
A misfire or rough-running complaint means the engine is not producing smooth, consistent power. A misfire means one or more cylinders isn't burning fuel properly, which causes shaking, a rough idle, hesitation or loss of power.

Note when it happens (cold start, idle, accelerating) and whether the check-engine light is on or flashing.

If the check-engine light is flashing or the car loses power, slow down and stop somewhere safe; a severe misfire can overheat and damage the catalytic converter.

turns.message: My check engine light is flashing
turns.answer:
A flashing (blinking) check-engine light usually means a severe misfire that can quickly overheat and damage the catalytic converter.

Reduce speed and load, stop in a safe place as soon as you can, and avoid continued driving until the vehicle is inspected or towed.

turns.message: The red oil pressure light came on while driving
turns.answer:
If the red oil-pressure light comes on while driving, stop safely and switch off the engine as soon as possible. Don't restart it until the oil level has been checked.

A red oil-pressure warning means the engine may not be getting enough oil pressure, which can damage it within minutes. Leaks and oil burning lower the oil level more gradually. Oil level, oil pressure, and oil condition are different checks.

If an oil-pressure warning appears while running, stop the engine as soon as it is safe.

turns.message: How do I check my engine oil?
turns.answer:
Check the oil with the car on level ground and the engine off, as the owner's manual describes: wait a few minutes, pull out the dipstick, wipe it, push it fully back in, then pull it out again and read the level between the marks.

Needing to top up often points to a leak or oil burning; have it checked. If it's low, add a little at a time using the oil grade in the owner's manual, then recheck; don't overfill.

If the red oil-pressure light comes on, stop the engine as soon as it's safe.

turns.message: How often should I change engine oil?
turns.answer:
For most cars, change the engine oil and filter every 5,000 to 10,000 km or every 6 months, whichever comes first. City traffic, short trips and heat count as severe service, so for a car driven in Metro Manila plan on about every 5,000 km; go longer only if the owner's manual or the oil-life monitor allows it.

Engine oil forms a lubricating film and helps manage friction and heat within the engine.

Check the oil level regularly between changes.

A routine oil-change reminder is not the same as an oil-pressure warning.

turns.message: My engine is making a knocking noise
turns.answer:
Engine noises point to different problems depending on the sound: knocking or pinging when accelerating, ticking from the top of the engine, rattling at start-up, or squealing from a belt.

Worn engine bearings (deep knocking).

Note when the noise happens (cold start, idle, accelerating) and whether it changes with engine speed.

A loud knock together with the oil-pressure light means switch the engine off as soon as it's safe.

turns.message: The engine cranks but won't start
turns.answer: If the engine cranks normally but won't start, it usually isn't getting fuel, spark or enough air, or the immobiliser is blocking it.

turns.message: Blue smoke from my exhaust
turns.answer:
Blue or blue-grey exhaust smoke means the engine is burning oil.

If the oil level drops quickly or the oil-pressure light comes on, stop driving.

turns.message: white smoke from exhaust
turns.answer:
Thin white vapour that clears once the engine warms up is usually just condensation. Thick white smoke that keeps coming, especially with a sweet smell, can mean coolant is burning in the engine; a failed head gasket is one possible cause. Thin white vapour for a few minutes after a cold start, especially in cool or humid weather, is usually water condensation in the exhaust and is normal.

On diesel engines, white smoke when cold can also be unburned fuel from faulty glow plugs, injectors, injection timing or low compression.

If the engine starts to overheat or the coolant level keeps dropping, stop driving and have it inspected.

turns.message: What does a timing belt do?
turns.answer: A timing belt or chain keeps the engine's valves and pistons in step. If it slips or breaks, the engine stops and can be badly damaged. Whether a vehicle uses a belt or chain, inspection and replacement requirements depend on the exact engine and manufacturer schedule.

turns.message: Car won't start, just clicking
turns.answer:
A car that won't start or cranks slowly usually has a weak battery, a poor battery connection, or a starter or charging problem.

Rapid clicking almost always means a flat battery or a poor connection: there isn't enough power to turn the starter. Try a jump start and check the terminals for looseness or white/green corrosion. Slow crank, clicking, dimming lights, battery/charging warning, repeated jump-start need, or stalling.

If you smell burning or see smoke from the wiring or battery, stop trying to start the car.

turns.message: What does an alternator do?
turns.answer:
The alternator supplies electrical power and charges the battery while the engine runs in vehicles equipped with one.

Starting and charging symptoms can involve the battery, starter, alternator, wiring, connections, or another electrical load.

turns.message: The battery light came on while driving
turns.answer:
Drive only as far as a safe place nearby, then stop; the car can lose power and stall when the battery runs down. If the temperature gauge also rises, stop straight away, because the same belt may drive the water pump.

A battery or charging light while driving means the charging system has a fault, usually an alternator that isn't charging, so the car is running on battery power and may stop.

turns.message: My battery dies overnight
turns.answer:
A car that won't start or cranks slowly usually has a weak battery, a poor battery connection, or a starter or charging problem.

Low battery charge or capacity, loose/corroded connections, charging-system faults, starter issues, or parasitic electrical draw.

With the engine off, check that the battery terminals are tight and free of corrosion.

If you smell burning or see smoke from the wiring or battery, stop trying to start the car.

turns.message: My radio stopped working, could it be a blown fuse?
turns.answer:
If a fuse blows again straight away there's a short circuit: don't fit a bigger fuse, have the wiring checked.

When one electrical item stops working, such as a light, the radio, a power outlet or a window, a blown fuse is a common cause.

One circuit stops working while the rest of the car is normal.

turns.message: I smell burning plastic from the dashboard
turns.answer:
A burning plastic or electrical smell can mean overheating wiring or a short circuit, which can start a fire. Pull over safely, switch off the engine and get everyone out of the car.

A slipping clutch or a dragging brake (burning rubber or acrid smell). A plastic bag stuck to the hot exhaust.

turns.message: How do I take care of my car battery?
turns.answer:
Keep the battery terminals clean and tight and avoid leaving lights or accessories on with the engine off. Most car batteries last about 2 to 4 years in a hot climate, so have it tested once it's around 3 years old or if starting becomes slower.

Replace the battery with the type and rating listed in the owner's manual. Short trips and long periods parked drain a battery; drive regularly or use a suitable maintainer.

turns.message: My brakes feel spongy
turns.answer:
A spongy or soft brake pedal usually means air in the brake lines, low brake fluid from a leak, or a failing master cylinder. It reduces braking power.

The pedal travels further than normal, feels soft, or sinks while held down.

A leaking caliper or brake hose.

A soft or sinking brake pedal is safety-critical: stop safely as soon as you can and arrange a tow instead of driving to a workshop.

turns.message: My brakes are not working while driving
turns.answer:
If your brakes fail while driving, pump the brake pedal firmly, shift to a lower gear, and apply the parking brake gradually while steering to a safe place. Turn on your hazard lights and use the horn to warn others.

Overheated brakes on a long descent (brake fade).

Once stopped, don't drive the car again; have it towed for inspection.

turns.message: my brakes are squeaking when I stop
turns.answer:
A squeak or squeal when braking is usually caused by the pads and rotors: worn pads touching their wear indicator, moisture or light rust, brake dust, or glazed friction surfaces.

Glazed or hardened pads or rotors after heavy braking or overheating.

A brief squeak on the first few stops in damp weather that then goes away is usually moisture.

Grinding or a metal-on-metal sound usually means the pads are worn through; stop driving when it's safe and have the brakes checked.

turns.message: grinding noise when I brake
turns.answer:
A grinding or metal-on-metal noise when braking usually means the pads are worn through and metal is rubbing the rotor, or something is caught in the brake.

A grinding noise that is also present when not braking can come from a worn wheel bearing.

Grinding brakes can lose stopping power and quickly damage the rotors: stop using the car and have it inspected or towed.

turns.message: What does the ABS light mean?
turns.answer: The ABS light means the anti-lock system has a fault. Normal braking usually still works, but the wheels can lock under hard braking. A red brake warning is more serious and can mean low brake fluid or a hydraulic problem. Brake and ABS warnings can indicate different systems.

turns.message: When should brake fluid be changed?
turns.answer:
Brake fluid transmits the pedal pressure to the brakes. It absorbs moisture over time, so it's replaced at the interval in the owner's manual. A slowly dropping level can be pad wear; a fast drop means a leak.

Use only the brake-fluid type printed on the reservoir cap or in the owner's manual.

turns.message: Car shakes when braking.
turns.answer:
Shaking or a pulsing pedal when braking usually means the brake rotors are uneven (often called warped), or there's a problem with the wheels, tires or suspension.

Loose wheel nuts or a damaged wheel or tire, which can shake at other times too.

Have the rotors measured during a brake inspection.

If the vibration is severe or braking feels weaker, stop driving and have the brakes checked.

turns.message: What do brake pads do?
turns.answer:
Brake pads press against a rotor or drum to create friction and slow the wheel. Rotors or drums provide the friction surface; calipers apply pad force in many disc-brake systems.

Brake pads and rotors wear with use. Squealing, grinding, vibration when braking or a longer stopping distance are signs they need inspecting. Noise or vibration can have several causes and requires inspection; it is not a measurement of remaining pad life.

turns.message: Transmission slipping
turns.answer:
Transmission slipping is when the engine revs rise but the car doesn't speed up as it should, or gears engage late or harshly. Slipping or delayed engagement describes a driving symptom, not a confirmed transmission failure.

If the car loses drive, the transmission smells burnt or an over-temperature warning appears, stop safely; continuing can cause major damage.

turns.message: How do I check transmission fluid?
turns.answer:
Transmission fluid lubricates, cools and operates the gearbox. Check and change it only as the owner's manual specifies; many modern automatics have no dipstick and need a workshop procedure.

Very dark or burnt-smelling fluid should be checked by a technician.

Have it checked at the next convenient service.

turns.message: How many liters of transmission fluid does my car need?
turns.answer: Transmission fluid lubricates, cools and operates the gearbox. Check and change it only as the owner's manual specifies; many modern automatics have no dipstick and need a workshop procedure.

turns.message: It's hard to shift gears in my manual car
turns.answer:
Difficulty selecting gears in a manual car usually comes from a clutch that isn't fully disengaging, low clutch fluid, worn synchronisers or a linkage problem.

Worn synchronisers (grinding when shifting). A worn or misadjusted gear linkage.

If you can't select a gear or the clutch pedal stays down, stop and arrange assistance.

turns.message: My transmission is whining
turns.answer: Whining, humming or clunking from the transmission can come from low fluid, worn bearings or gears, worn mounts or driveline parts.

turns.message: My steering is heavy
turns.answer:
Steering that suddenly becomes heavy usually means power-steering assistance has been reduced or lost, or a front tire is low.

Worn or binding steering or suspension joints.

If steering becomes hard while driving, slow down, hold the wheel firmly and stop somewhere safe. Don't continue if steering is difficult or unpredictable.

turns.message: I lost steering while driving
turns.answer:
After a steering failure while driving, don't drive the car again until it has been inspected; arrange a tow.

If you lose steering control while driving, stay calm, hold the wheel, turn on the hazard lights, ease off the accelerator and brake gently and steadily to stop. Don't brake hard or swerve.

If the car is parked and the wheel won't turn with the key, the steering lock is probably engaged: turn the wheel gently left and right while turning the key or pressing the start button.

turns.message: My steering wheel is locked and the key won't turn
turns.answer:
If you lose steering control while driving, stay calm, hold the wheel, turn on the hazard lights, ease off the accelerator and brake gently and steadily to stop. Don't brake hard or swerve.

The wheel won't turn, turns without the car responding, or becomes extremely heavy.

A seized or locked steering column.

If the car is parked and the wheel won't turn with the key, the steering lock is probably engaged: turn the wheel gently left and right while turning the key or pressing the start button.

After a steering failure while driving, don't drive the car again until it has been inspected; arrange a tow.

turns.message: My car keeps bouncing after bumps
turns.answer:
Worn shock absorbers or struts make the car keep bouncing after bumps, dive when braking and lean more in corners, and they can lengthen stopping distances.

Bouncing, nose-dive under braking, knocking over bumps.

turns.message: My steering wheel is not straight when driving straight
turns.answer: Wheel alignment sets the angles of the wheels. Signs it's off include pulling to one side, a crooked steering wheel when driving straight, and uneven tire wear.

turns.message: Car pulls to the left.
turns.answer:
A car that pulls or drifts to one side usually has uneven tire pressure, wheel misalignment, a dragging brake or a worn steering or suspension part.

A sticking brake caliper or brake hose problem (pulling mainly when braking, sometimes with a hot wheel or burning smell).

Note whether it pulls all the time or only when braking; pulling only when braking points to the brakes.

If the pull is sudden or strong, or happens when braking, have it inspected before driving further.

turns.message: My steering wheel shakes at high speed
turns.answer:
A steering wheel that shakes at higher speeds is most often caused by unbalanced wheels, and sometimes by a damaged tire, a bent wheel or worn steering parts.

Worn tie-rod ends, ball joints, wheel bearings or other steering and suspension parts.

Avoid high speeds until the cause is found.

If the vibration is sudden or severe, slow down and stop safely; a tire may be failing.

turns.message: Clicking noise when turning
turns.answer:
A clicking or popping noise when turning is most often a worn outer CV joint on a front-wheel-drive car, usually after its rubber boot has torn. Other parts can also make noises when turning, so it needs an inspection to confirm.

Note which side the noise comes from and whether it happens turning left, right or both.

turns.message: My car suddenly started shaking violently
turns.answer:
Sudden, severe shaking can mean a tire is failing, a wheel is loose, or there's a serious engine or drivetrain fault. Slow down gradually and stop somewhere safe.

Shaking through the whole car, steering wheel or seat that appears suddenly.

turns.message: Whining noise when turning the steering wheel
turns.answer:
A whining or groaning noise when turning the wheel on a car with hydraulic power steering often means low power-steering fluid or a worn pump.

Whining that rises when turning, sometimes with heavier steering.

If the steering also becomes heavy, drive carefully to a safe place and have it inspected.

turns.message: I smell gasoline near the car
turns.answer:
A strong fuel smell or a fuel leak is a fire risk. Don't start or keep running the engine, keep away from ignition sources such as sparks, flames and cigarettes, and move away from the car.

For a strong or lasting smell, or any dripping fuel, have the car towed for inspection instead of driving it. If the smell is faint and only right after refuelling, check that the fuel cap is closed properly.

turns.message: There is smoke coming from under the hood
turns.answer:
Smoke from under the bonnet can be steam from overheating coolant, oil burning on hot parts, or an electrical fire. Pull over safely, switch off the engine and get everyone out of the car.

Don't open the bonnet while smoke is coming out; opening it can feed a fire.

turns.message: Can I open the high-voltage battery pack?
turns.answer:
Hybrid and electric cars use high-voltage systems that can cause a fatal electric shock. Never open, touch or cut the orange high-voltage cables or the battery pack.

Do not open a traction-battery enclosure, touch orange cables/connectors, probe high-voltage terminals, defeat an interlock, or attempt isolation yourself.

After a crash, or if you see smoke, smell burning or hear hissing from the battery, move away from the vehicle and call emergency services.

turns.message: What coolant should I use?
turns.answer:
Top up only with the coolant type in the owner's manual; don't mix types unless it allows it.

Never open the radiator or reservoir cap on a hot engine.

turns.message: When should I service my car?
turns.answer: Compare the odometer and the date of the last service with the schedule in the owner's manual. Compare dated service records and odometer readings with the exact vehicle's official schedule.

turns.message: When do I replace the air filter?
turns.answer:
Air, cabin and fuel filters, spark plugs and other wear items are replaced at intervals set by the vehicle maker, by distance or time.

The engine air filter limits intake contaminants. The cabin air filter cleans air entering the passenger compartment where fitted.

Replace the engine air filter sooner if you drive in dusty conditions.

turns.message: My aircon is blowing warm air
turns.answer:
Weak or warm air from the A/C usually comes from low refrigerant, a compressor problem, a blocked cabin filter or condenser, or a blower or control fault. A warm vent or weak airflow does not by itself identify a failed compressor or refrigerant leak.

Warm air with normal airflow can involve control settings, blend-door operation, heat-source availability, refrigerant-circuit performance, or a sensor/control fault.

Check whether air is blowing strongly; weak airflow points to the blower or cabin filter rather than the refrigerant.

turns.message: What is P0420?
turns.answer:
P0420: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1. Common causes: catalyst aged or poisoned (oil consumption, silicone, coolant); catalyst overheated by misfire or rich running; rear oxygen sensor sluggish, dirty or unsuitable. Typical signs: check engine light on, otherwise often no change in driving; emission test failed (higher HC, CO, NOx). This code normally turns on the check-engine (MIL) light.

A code shows which circuit or test failed, so confirm the cause with an inspection before replacing parts.

turns.message: What does code P0300 mean?
turns.answer:
P0300: Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected. Common causes: false air (vacuum leak, crankcase ventilation, intake gasket); worn or wrong spark plugs on several cylinders, faulty ignition coils; fuel pressure too low or high, contaminated fuel. Typical signs: check engine light on, flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate; rough idle, jerking, vibration. This code normally turns on the check-engine (MIL) light. Reduced-power (limp) mode is possible.

A code shows which circuit or test failed, so confirm the cause with an inspection before replacing parts.

P0171: System Too Lean Bank 1. Common causes: air leak after the air flow sensor (intake manifold gasket, vacuum hoses, throttle body gasket, brake booster line); crankcase ventilation leaking or faulty (PCV hose, diaphragm in valve cover, oil cap, dipstick); air flow sensor dirty or drifting (measures too little air). Typical signs: check engine light on (after two drive cycles); rough or unsteady idle, possibly stalling. This code normally turns on the check-engine (MIL) light.

A code shows which circuit or test failed, so confirm the cause with an inspection before replacing parts.

turns.message: What is P0300?
turns.answer:
P0300: Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected. Common causes: false air (vacuum leak, crankcase ventilation, intake gasket); worn or wrong spark plugs on several cylinders, faulty ignition coils; fuel pressure too low or high, contaminated fuel. Typical signs: check engine light on, flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate; rough idle, jerking, vibration. This code normally turns on the check-engine (MIL) light. Reduced-power (limp) mode is possible.

A code shows which circuit or test failed, so confirm the cause with an inspection before replacing parts.

turns.message: What causes it?
turns.answer:
The usual causes of P0300 are: false air (vacuum leak, crankcase ventilation, intake gasket); worn or wrong spark plugs on several cylinders, faulty ignition coils; fuel pressure too low or high, contaminated fuel; valve timing (stretched chain), valves, compression on several cylinders; false detection: tone wheel or pulley, rough road, vibration, software.

Confirm the cause with an inspection or tests before replacing parts.

turns.message: What is P1456?
turns.answer: P1456 is not in the generic OBD-II code list. Codes like P1xxx, B1xxx or U1xxx are usually manufacturer-specific: tell me the make, model and year, or check the manufacturer's service information or a scan tool that supports that brand.

turns.message: What is the difference between P0 and P1 codes?
turns.answer: OBD-II codes have five characters. The letter shows the system: P for powertrain, B for body, C for chassis and U for network. P0 and P2 codes are generic, P1 codes are manufacturer-specific, and P3 codes are split between generic and manufacturer-specific.

turns.message: What does the check engine light mean?
turns.answer: Warning lights mean a system needs attention. Red lights (oil pressure, temperature, brakes, charging) usually mean stop soon; amber lights such as the check-engine light mean get it checked soon.

turns.message: What should I check before renting a car?
turns.answer:
Check the tires, lights and wipers, and that no warning lights stay on after starting. Report any damage or fault to the rental team before driving off.

Don't drive or rent out a car with a safety-related fault such as damaged tires, a brake warning or faulty lights.

turns.message: I scratched the rental car, what should I do?
turns.answer: Scratches, dents, broken glass or lights found during or after a rental.

turns.message: There's a warning light on my rental car
turns.answer:
If something seems wrong with a rental car, tell the rental team straight away: what you noticed, when it started, any warning lights and the mileage. Don't arrange repairs yourself unless they ask you to.

Note the exact warning light or symptom and take a photo of the dashboard if it's safe to do so.

If the fault affects brakes, steering, tires, overheating or oil pressure, stop driving and wait for instructions.

turns.message: My car makes a noise
turns.answer: What kind of noise is it, and when does it happen? For example: squealing when braking, clicking when turning, knocking from the engine, or a hum that gets louder with speed.

turns.message: Something is wrong with my car
turns.answer: What's happening with the car? Tell me the symptom, for example a noise, a warning light, a smell, a leak, or trouble starting, steering or braking.

turns.message: My car smells weird
turns.answer: What does it smell like, and where is it coming from? For example: burning plastic, fuel, a sweet coolant smell or burnt oil. If it's a burning or fuel smell, stop somewhere safe first.

turns.message: A light came on on my dashboard
turns.answer: Which warning light is it, and what colour? For example: the check-engine light (steady or flashing), the battery light, the oil-pressure light, or the brake or ABS light.

turns.message: My car makes a strange noise
turns.answer: What kind of noise is it, and when does it happen? For example: squealing when braking, clicking when turning, knocking from the engine, or a hum that gets louder with speed.

turns.message: It squeals when I brake
turns.answer:
A squeak or squeal when braking is usually caused by the pads and rotors: worn pads touching their wear indicator, moisture or light rust, brake dust, or glazed friction surfaces.

Glazed or hardened pads or rotors after heavy braking or overheating.

A squeal that is constant or getting louder should be inspected soon.

Grinding or a metal-on-metal sound usually means the pads are worn through; stop driving when it's safe and have the brakes checked.

turns.message: Why is my car overheating?
turns.answer:
Overheating means the cooling system isn't removing heat fast enough, or coolant isn't circulating properly. An overheating indication means heat is not being removed or circulated as intended, or the temperature reading is not trustworthy.

A coolant-pump circulation or drive problem can reduce coolant flow and cause overheating at different speeds; leaks or noise may be present but are not required.

If the gauge is in the red or you see steam, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Never open the radiator cap while the engine is hot; hot coolant can cause severe burns.

turns.message: What about a flat tire?
turns.answer:
If your tire is flat, slow down gradually and pull over somewhere safe, away from traffic. Turn on your hazard lights and don't keep driving on the flat tire. Driving on a flat tire quickly destroys it and can damage the wheel and make the car hard to control.

A leaking valve or a poor seal between the tire and the rim.

turns.message: My steering is heavy
turns.answer:
Steering that suddenly becomes heavy usually means power-steering assistance has been reduced or lost, or a front tire is low.

Worn or binding steering or suspension joints.

If steering becomes hard while driving, slow down, hold the wheel firmly and stop somewhere safe. Don't continue if steering is difficult or unpredictable.

turns.message: Is it safe to drive?
turns.answer: Not until it's checked. Heavy steering makes the car harder to control, especially in an emergency, so drive only as far as a safe place and have it inspected.

turns.message: Transmission slipping
turns.answer:
Transmission slipping is when the engine revs rise but the car doesn't speed up as it should, or gears engage late or harshly. Slipping or delayed engagement describes a driving symptom, not a confirmed transmission failure.

If the car loses drive, the transmission smells burnt or an over-temperature warning appears, stop safely; continuing can cause major damage.

turns.message: How much will it cost to fix?
turns.answer: Start with the fluid level and condition, which is cheap to check. A fluid service is moderate; a solenoid or valve-body repair costs more; a rebuild or replacement is the most expensive repair on most cars.

turns.message: Car won't start, just clicking
turns.answer:
A car that won't start or cranks slowly usually has a weak battery, a poor battery connection, or a starter or charging problem.

Rapid clicking almost always means a flat battery or a poor connection: there isn't enough power to turn the starter. Try a jump start and check the terminals for looseness or white/green corrosion. Slow crank, clicking, dimming lights, battery/charging warning, repeated jump-start need, or stalling.

If you smell burning or see smoke from the wiring or battery, stop trying to start the car.

turns.message: The battery is new
turns.answer: A new battery can still be discharged or poorly connected, so check that the terminals are clean and tight; if they are, a starter-motor or relay fault is the next most likely cause.

turns.message: My engine is misfiring
turns.answer:
A misfire or rough-running complaint means the engine is not producing smooth, consistent power. A misfire means one or more cylinders isn't burning fuel properly, which causes shaking, a rough idle, hesitation or loss of power.

Note when it happens (cold start, idle, accelerating) and whether the check-engine light is on or flashing.

If the check-engine light is flashing or the car loses power, slow down and stop somewhere safe; a severe misfire can overheat and damage the catalytic converter.

turns.message: What else could it be?
turns.answer:
Fuel injectors meter fuel into the engine according to the engine-control system.

A flashing check-engine light means a severe misfire. Drive gently to a safe stop; unburnt fuel can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter.

A flashing engine warning light, severe shaking, fuel smell, or stalling can indicate a condition that may damage the vehicle or create a hazard.

turns.message: What is the torque for the wheel nuts on my car?
turns.answer:
Worn suspension or steering parts, loose wheel nuts or wheel and tire problems can make it worse. Shaking or a pulsing pedal when braking usually means the brake rotors are uneven (often called warped), or there's a problem with the wheels, tires or suspension.

Loose wheel nuts or a damaged wheel or tire, which can shake at other times too.

If wheels were recently removed, have the wheel-nut tightness checked before driving far.

turns.message: How many liters of oil does my engine take?
turns.answer:
Use the oil grade (viscosity, such as 0W-20 or 5W-30) and the specification (such as API SP or ILSAC GF-6) listed in the owner's manual or on the oil filler cap. The grade matters more than the brand.

Engine oil lubricates and cools the moving parts and carries dirt to the oil filter.

Fully synthetic oil protects better in heat and stop-and-go traffic and is required by many newer engines; use it if the manual says so. Diesel engines need oil rated for diesel (for example API CK-4 or the maker's specification), so don't swap gasoline and diesel oils unless the oil is rated for both.

turns.message: the car feels like it's floating over bumps
turns.answer:
Worn shock absorbers or struts make the car keep bouncing after bumps, dive when braking and lean more in corners, and they can lengthen stopping distances.

Bouncing, nose-dive under braking, knocking over bumps.

turns.message: what's that orange engine symbol on my dash
turns.answer:
Warning lights mean a system needs attention. Red lights (oil pressure, temperature, brakes, charging) usually mean stop soon; amber lights such as the check-engine light mean get it checked soon.

Look up the exact symbol in the owner's manual.

turns.message: my headlights are dim and the car died
turns.answer:
A battery or charging light while driving means the charging system has a fault, usually an alternator that isn't charging, so the car is running on battery power and may stop.

Drive only as far as a safe place nearby, then stop; the car can lose power and stall when the battery runs down. If the temperature gauge also rises, stop straight away, because the same belt may drive the water pump.

turns.message: car vibrates when I idle at a red light
turns.answer:
Shaking at idle usually means the engine is running unevenly, often from a misfire, or that worn engine mounts are letting normal engine vibration through to the cabin.

A dirty throttle body or an idle-control fault.

Notice whether it gets worse with the A/C on, or in Drive compared with Park; that points towards the engine mounts or idle control.

If the check-engine light is flashing or the engine shakes hard, stop driving and have it checked; a severe misfire can damage the catalytic converter.

turns.message: the AC smells musty
turns.answer:
A musty or mouldy smell from the vents usually comes from moisture and mould on the A/C evaporator, or a dirty cabin air filter.

If the smell stays, a workshop can clean the evaporator and check the drain.

turns.message: can I use water instead of coolant
turns.answer:
Plain water can be used briefly in an emergency to get the car to a workshop, but it doesn't protect the engine against corrosion, freezing or boiling the way coolant does.

Using water instead of coolant.

Have the system drained and refilled with the coolant type in the owner's manual as soon as you can.

Never open the radiator or reservoir cap on a hot engine.

turns.message: my car jerks when shifting from 2nd to 3rd
turns.answer:
Engine speed rises without expected acceleration, delayed engagement, harsh shifts, warning messages, or unusual noise.

If the car loses drive, the transmission smells burnt or an over-temperature warning appears, stop safely; continuing can cause major damage.

turns.message: I hear a humming noise that gets louder with speed
turns.answer:
A hum or growl that gets louder with speed, and changes when you turn one way, is the classic sign of a worn wheel bearing. A grinding noise when turning can also come from a stone in the brake shield or a worn CV joint.

Note whether the noise gets louder when turning left or right: a bearing usually gets louder on the opposite side from the turn.

turns.message: i ran over a nail
turns.answer:
If your tire is flat, slow down gradually and pull over somewhere safe, away from traffic. Turn on your hazard lights and don't keep driving on the flat tire.

A nail, screw or other object in the tread.

turns.message: what does a catalytic converter do
turns.answer:
A catalytic converter and, where fitted, a diesel particulate filter treat or capture specified exhaust constituents. The catalytic converter uses precious-metal catalysts to turn harmful exhaust gases (carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides) into less harmful ones.

The exhaust system carries combustion gases away and may include oxygen sensors, a catalytic converter, exhaust-gas recirculation, and diesel aftertreatment such as a particulate filter.

turns.message: my brake pedal is hard to press
turns.answer:
A brake pedal that's hard to press usually means the brake booster isn't assisting, often because of a vacuum leak or a failed booster. The brakes still work, but they need much more force.

Note whether the pedal is hard only with the engine off; it's normal for the pedal to be firm after a few presses with the engine off.

Braking needs much more effort and stopping distances get longer, so drive carefully to a safe place and have it inspected before driving normally.

turns.message: engine temperature warning light
turns.answer:
Treat a high-temperature warning as real until the vehicle-specific checks establish otherwise.

A heater that turns cold while the engine temperature rises can accompany low coolant or interrupted circulation and is an urgent warning, but heater design and control vary.

Record when the temperature rises, warning messages, coolant level only when cold, visible residue, cabin-heater behavior, recent repairs, and ambient/load conditions. Do not run an overheating engine to reproduce the symptom.

If the gauge is in the red or you see steam, pull over safely and switch off the engine. Never open the radiator cap while the engine is hot; hot coolant can cause severe burns.

turns.message: what should i do now?
turns.answer:
Once the engine has fully cooled, check the coolant level in the reservoir. Check whether the radiator fan runs when the engine gets hot or when the A/C is switched on.

If a high-temperature warning appears, steam or coolant is expelled, or the temperature continues to rise, stop safely and switch off the engine.

turns.message: how much will that cost
turns.answer: A cap, hose or thermostat is a small job; a fan motor or water pump costs more; a head gasket is a big job, so stop driving as soon as it overheats.

turns.answer:

Note when it happens (cold start, idle, accelerating) and whether the check-engine light is on or flashing.

If the check-engine light is flashing or the car loses power, slow down and stop somewhere safe; a severe misfire can overheat and damage the catalytic converter.

turns.message: I already replaced the spark plugs
turns.answer:
If the coils are fine, check the spark plugs, fuel injectors and for air leaks, then compression. With new spark plugs, an ignition coil, a fuel injector, an air leak or low compression are the more likely causes; a code such as P0301 to P0306 shows which cylinder to test.

Spark plugs are cheap; an ignition coil is a moderate part, and a good shop swaps coils between cylinders to prove which one is bad before replacing. Injector or compression problems cost much more.

turns.message: my car won't start
turns.answer:
A car that won't start or cranks slowly usually has a weak battery, a poor battery connection, or a starter or charging problem.

If you smell burning or see smoke from the wiring or battery, stop trying to start the car.

turns.message: the lights work fine though
turns.answer: Rapid clicking with dim lights usually points to a weak battery or poor connection; a single click with bright lights can point to the starter. Record warning lights and whether the problem occurs after the vehicle sits or while running.

P0128: Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature). Common causes: thermostat stuck open or opening too early; coolant sensor reading too low, or corrosion and resistance in its circuit; low coolant level or air in the system. Typical signs: check engine light on; temperature gauge stays low or drops while driving. This code normally turns on the check-engine (MIL) light.

A code shows which circuit or test failed, so confirm the cause with an inspection before replacing parts.

turns.message: is it serious?
turns.answer: P0128 normally turns on the check-engine light. A steady check-engine light usually means have it checked soon rather than stop straight away. If the light starts flashing, or the car overheats, loses power or drives abnormally, stop when it's safe and arrange an inspection.

turns.message: my rental car has a check engine light, what do I do
turns.answer:
Warning lights mean a system needs attention. Red lights (oil pressure, temperature, brakes, charging) usually mean stop soon; amber lights such as the check-engine light mean get it checked soon.

As it's a rental car, tell the rental team before arranging any repairs.
